text: Every data scientist has shipped a number that turned out to be wrong. Usually it wasn't a dramatic crash — a join quietly duplicated rows, a filter dropped the wrong category, or a small tweak to a cleaning function changed a total nobody re-checked. Tests are how you catch those mistakes before your stakeholders do. The good news: a test is just a small function that checks one behavior and fails loudly when it's wrong.

A test has three parts: arrange some small input, act by calling your function, and assert the result is what you expect. test_add_revenue_multiplies_quantity_and_price builds a two-row DataFrame and asserts the revenue column comes out as 10.0 and 12.0. test_add_revenue_does_not_change_input calls the function and then asserts the original DataFrame still has no revenue column at all.

Notice the names — each one says what behavior is expected, so when a test fails, the name tells you what broke. Save these in tests slash test_cleaning.py, and a runner called pytest discovers every function whose name starts with test underscore and reports which passed and failed. Install it with pip install pytest, run pytest from the project folder — all five tests passed against last lesson's module.

Now suppose someone refactors add_revenue and accidentally types a plus sign instead of a multiplication sign. On our sample rows that produces 7.0 and 7.0 instead of 10.0 and 12.0, so the assertion fails immediately. Without the test, that wrong revenue would flow silently into every chart downstream, and nobody would know until a stakeholder asked why the numbers looked off.

When the result is a whole table, pandas.testing.assert_frame_equal compares columns, order, values, and dtypes all at once, and raises an error describing exactly where they differ if they don't match. test_clean_orders_full_output builds one raw row and one expected row, then asserts the full pipeline output matches it exactly.

Tests check your code using small, made-up inputs you control. Data checks examine the real data each time it arrives, and they use similar tools. After cleaning the real file, you might assert that order_id is unique and that every revenue value is non-negative — both passed on our sample. In production, a failing data check stops the pipeline before bad numbers spread.

You can't test everything, so prioritize three things: business rules like revenue, discounts, and status logic, where wrong numbers cost the most; edge cases like empty input, missing values, and duplicates — our standardize_region leaves a missing region missing rather than crashing; and bugs you've already fixed, so they never quietly return.

To recap: a test arranges input, acts, and asserts, with a name that states the expected behavior. Plain assert plus assert_frame_equal covers most data-code tests. Tests protect your functions; data checks protect against bad incoming data. Start with business rules, edge cases, and past bugs. Next up: reproducibility — making sure your results come out the same every time.
